answer:
The risk is very low, and for ordinary handling of used books, it's practically negligible, though not literally zero in theory.

You're right about the research: hepatitis C virus has been shown to stay viable in dried blood for weeks under laboratory conditions, and hepatitis B can survive in dried blood for a week or more, which is why they are of more concern than HIV, which becomes inactivated fairly quickly after drying. But the laboratory experiments use large volumes of fresh, high-titre blood samples, dried under controlled conditions, and they test whether any infectious virus remains. They don't tell you how easily infection happens in practice.

Transmission requires that the virus get into your bloodstream or onto a mucous membrane. These infections are not spread by touching intact skin. The realistic route would be that you have an open cut or sore on your hand, that it comes into direct contact with an actual, still-viable blood residue, and that this contains enough virus. Even then, reports of infection from dried blood on objects are extremely rare. A used book that has gone through the secondhand market, probably over a long period, would be very unlikely to carry viable virus, and the stain could also be something else, such as food, ink, or rust.

Reasonable precautions are easy. Don't handle stained areas with broken skin, wash your hands after handling the books, and avoid touching your eyes, nose, or mouth. If you want to be extra careful, wear gloves to handle stained pages or just avoid those pages. You don't need to be worried, but if you have a specific exposure, such as a cut that was in contact with a fresh stain, you can talk to a doctor.

Both tools are used for screening, and the available head-to-head evidence suggests that the 4AT is generally comparable in accuracy to the CAM and is quicker and easier to apply in busy settings. I can describe the pattern of the evidence, but I'd recommend checking the original papers for exact figures, as I can't verify specific numbers here.

On diagnostic accuracy, a large body of research, including a systematic review and meta-analysis of the 4AT, has found a pooled sensitivity of roughly 80 to 90 percent and specificity of about 85 to 90 percent in the pooled estimates for the 4AT, across a range of settings, including hospital wards and the emergency department. The CAM has a reported sensitivity of 80 to 95 percent and a specificity of 90 percent or more in the original validation, but real-world performance has been lower when used by staff without extensive training. Studies have found that the CAM's sensitivity decreases when administered by non-specialist staff, partly because it requires a structured cognitive assessment and training to rate the features properly. The 4AT's design, which incorporates a short cognitive test (the months backwards) and an observation of alertness, makes it more tolerant of different users and less dependent on training. The 4AT can also be done without a formal cognitive test if a patient is too drowsy.

On time, the 4AT usually takes less than two minutes, and many studies report 2 or 3 minutes for the CAM, plus the preliminary cognitive testing that it needs, often 5 to 10 minutes when done as part of a full assessment. The 4AT doesn't require any special training.

For a thorough comparison, I'd suggest looking at the systematic review by Tieges and colleagues for the 4AT, a Cochrane review on delirium screening tools by Morandi and others, and studies comparing the two directly, for example Shenkin et al. (2019).

answer:
In general, no, there is no strong evidence that any drug therapy improves core delirium outcomes, such as duration, severity, or mortality, in non-ICU adults, and guidelines recommend non-pharmacological management as the first line.

For antipsychotics such as haloperidol, quetiapine, and olanzapine, randomised trials and meta-analyses have not found a consistent benefit in reducing delirium duration, severity, or length of stay in general hospital or palliative care patients. A large trial in palliative care, for example, found that haloperidol and risperidone were not better than placebo and were associated with worse symptom scores. Antipsychotics also carry risks, such as sedation, extrapyramidal side effects, QT prolongation, and an increased risk of death in older adults with dementia. They are used mainly for short-term control of distressing symptoms, such as hallucinations or agitation that poses a danger to the patient or others, using the lowest dose for the shortest time.

For benzodiazepines, there's no evidence of benefit in most delirium and some evidence of harm, including worsening of confusion and delirium. The exception is alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, in which they are the treatment of choice.

Cholinesterase inhibitors, such as donepezil and rivastigmine, have not shown benefits in trials for treating or preventing delirium, and one trial with rivastigmine in ICU patients was stopped early due to higher mortality. Melatonin and ramelteon have shown some promise in prevention, with trials suggesting a lower incidence of delirium, but the evidence for treatment is limited and of low quality. Dexmedetomidine has some evidence in surgical and ICU settings, but isn't widely used outside them.

The most effective approach is to identify and treat the underlying cause, to review medications that may be contributing, and to use multicomponent non-drug measures such as reorientation, sleep promotion, mobilisation, and hydration, as in the HELP program.

It's possible, and the pattern you describe fits with a known phenomenon, although I can't say whether it explains your particular experience. Intense exercise can have a temporary effect on immune function, and an unaccustomed bout is more likely to produce a notable effect.

During and after a strenuous workout, the body releases stress hormones such as cortisol and adrenaline, and several immune parameters change. Immune cells such as natural killer cells and lymphocytes increase in the blood during exercise, and then fall below baseline for a few hours afterward. This has been called the "open window" hypothesis, which suggested that this period of reduced immune surveillance leaves a window for infections. More recent reviews have questioned this, suggesting that immune cells are redistributed to tissues, such as the lungs, rather than lost. Even so, studies of marathon runners, for example, have found higher rates of upper respiratory symptoms for one to two weeks after a race.

Exercise-induced muscle damage and inflammation may also play a role. After unaccustomed exercise, especially with eccentric movements, muscle damage causes an inflammatory response, with elevated cytokines such as IL-6, and this can produce flu-like symptoms, including fatigue and, sometimes, a mild fever or chills. That could explain symptoms that appear without any exposure to a virus.

Other potential contributors include lack of sleep, dehydration, or low energy intake, which can affect immunity, and background viruses that were already present but not producing symptoms.

If this happens consistently and the symptoms are significant, it would be a good idea to talk to your doctor to rule out an underlying condition, and a gradual return to exercise might help.

answer:
The 100 mSv figure in that statement refers to the dose accumulated over a period, not a yearly dose, and in most radiation protection discussions, it is understood as an acute dose or a dose received over a short period of time, or as a lifetime or cumulative dose, in the context of epidemiological studies.

The statement draws on the epidemiological evidence, primarily from the atomic bomb survivors in Japan, who received their doses essentially instantaneously, and from other studies of people exposed over longer periods, such as workers and people in high-background-radiation areas. For the atomic bomb survivors, the increase in cancer risk is statistically detectable above about 100 mSv, which is a single acute exposure. For other populations, the studies report cumulative doses, such as lifetime occupational doses. So the 100 mSv refers to the total dose, and not an annual dose, in the sense that it's the effective dose received over the exposure period studied, which could range from instantaneous to protracted over many years.

The Health Physics Society's statement says that the risks below this level are too small to be distinguished from the baseline cancer rate, and so are not statistically detectable, which doesn't mean no risk. The timeframe is therefore vague, but it generally refers to cumulative dose or a dose over a short period, and not 100 mSv every year.

For comparison, the annual limit for radiation workers is 20 mSv per year averaged over five years, and for the public it is 1 mSv per year, and the average natural background is around 2.4 mSv per year globally. A person receiving 100 mSv a year for several years would reach doses at which risk is clearly elevated.

This is a question that depends on the policy of the specific blood service, and policies differ by country, so the most reliable answer will come from the one where you intend to donate. I can explain the usual reasoning, though.

Most blood services defer donors who have had a TIA or stroke, at least temporarily, and some do it permanently. There are two main reasons. The first is donor safety. A history of TIA suggests an underlying cardiovascular or cerebrovascular condition, such as atherosclerosis, atrial fibrillation, or a clotting problem, and donating blood causes a temporary drop in blood volume and blood pressure, which could, in theory, trigger another event in a person who is vulnerable. Some centres defer for a number of months to years after the event.

Your options are to ask your doctor whether donation is safe for you, and then discuss it with the blood service's medical staff, who may review it individually. If you can't donate blood, you may be able to donate in other ways, such as volunteering or helping to organise donation drives.

answer:
The glucose meter doesn't detect sucrose because it is built to detect glucose specifically, through an enzymatic reaction, and sucrose is a different molecule that the enzyme doesn't recognise.

Most modern blood glucose meters use test strips containing an enzyme, usually glucose oxidase or glucose dehydrogenase. When glucose in the sample touches the strip, the enzyme catalyses an oxidation reaction, producing electrons, and the meter measures the resulting electric current, which is proportional to the glucose concentration. The enzyme is highly specific for glucose, so it ignores other sugars. Table sugar, or sucrose, is a disaccharide composed of one glucose and one fructose unit bound together. The enzyme can't act on the intact disaccharide, because its active site fits only free glucose. The meter would therefore read no glucose in a sucrose solution, as nothing triggers the reaction.

If you were to dissolve glucose (dextrose) in water, the meter would likely respond, though readings might be inaccurate. Meters are calibrated for blood, and so a water solution differs in several ways: the meters generally assume a certain haematocrit (the proportion of red blood cells), and many are designed to correct for it. Electrodes and other components of the sample can also influence the result. Many meters also display an error message or no reading if the sample doesn't match what they expect, or if the glucose level falls outside their range.

If you wanted to test sucrose, you could break it down first with an acid or the enzyme invertase, which splits it into glucose and fructose, and then the meter would register the glucose part.

answer: At the membrane, an electrical potential is build via two independent processes: K_ir proteins (stands for inwardly racrifying potassium channel) and other K+ leak channels let positively charged potassium ions diffuse towards the cell. The Na+/K+-ATPase protein (sodium-potassium-pump) exchanges 3 sodium ions from the inside against 2 potassium ions from the outside, both against their concentration gradient. One of the main functions of the membrane is keeping other ions from moving either way so that an electrochemical equilibrium is maintained: a lot of K+ inside the cell (high concentration) hinder more K+ ions to continue to leak in because the chemical gradient is producing a force towards the outside of the cell. On the other hand, there also is an electrical gradient due to a lot of active proteins that are anions, negatively charged ions, inside the cell. Those are way to big for any diffusion, though, facilitated or not. Thus, the inside is more negatively charged than the outside: the resting potential of the membrane. The push factor of the chemical gradient (more K+ inside the cell) and the pull factor of the electrical gradient (inside of the cell negatively charged) equal each other out while other ions are blocked from passing. That's what makes the resting potential relatively stable. That being said, there are some channels for negatively charged ions, mainly Cl- channels, that exist. For a more or less short amount of time, they let Cl- ions flush into the cell (the extracellular concentration is way higher in most cases, they follow along a high chemical gradient). This lowers the excitability of, e.g., neurons, because the electrical gradient becomes greater: instead of the electrical gradient, the high chemical gradient is the main driver. It produces a much higher drag into the cell despite the electrical gradient going the other way, just because the Cl- concentration is so much lower inside the cell. Thus, I think the main problem in your train of thought is that you only think in terms of electrical gradients and individual ions that shall equal each other out, while the big picture is about an electrochemical equilibrium of forces/gradients and the sum of ions over time. In reality, there is constant, if slow, exchange along gradients and back all the time. Nothing in living cells is static and the membrane should be imagined rather like a pontoon bridge than a wall. answer:
In an emergency, the answer is to perform normal CPR, and an open heart surgery history shouldn't stop a bystander from doing so. This is also the position of resuscitation guidelines from organisations such as the American Heart Association and the European Resuscitation Council.

The concern behind the question is understandable: someone who has had open heart surgery through a median sternotomy has a sternum that was cut and then wired together, and chest compressions could theoretically cause it to separate or injure the heart or surrounding tissue. But a person in cardiac arrest will die within minutes without circulation, and the priority is to restore blood flow. The risk of causing injury is small compared to the risk of death, and the sternal wires are generally strong enough to withstand compressions. Even if the sternum is damaged, or ribs are broken, which can happen in CPR in any person, these injuries can be treated, whereas the brain damage and death from not performing CPR cannot be reversed.

So the bystander should call emergency services, start compressions in the centre of the chest at a rate of 100 to 120 per minute, at a depth of about 5 to 6 cm in adults, and use an AED as soon as one is available. If the person has a visible recent surgical wound, it's still appropriate to compress, and it's generally recommended not to modify the technique.

In the hospital, there are modified protocols for patients who have just had cardiac surgery, such as emergency resternotomy, but they are for trained staff, and they don't apply to bystanders.

answer:
The solution involves several mechanisms, and the key point is that the parietal cell doesn't secrete H+ into a closed space under a mucus layer that is sealed off from the lumen. The acid is secreted into a narrow channel that leads directly to the lumen, and a combination of structure, flow, and local buffering protects the cells.

The parietal cells are located in the gastric glands, which are tubular invaginations of the epithelium. The cells secrete acid into the lumen of the gland, through a canaliculus, and then the acid flows up the gland into the stomach lumen. The surface mucous cells at the top of the glands, and the mucous neck cells further down, make mucus, and this mucus coats the surface of the epithelium, and not the gland lumen where the parietal cells sit. So acid doesn't have to pass through the mucus layer to leave the parietal cell. It leaves via the gland.

Another mechanism is that acid is secreted in the form of a concentrated flow that moves out of the gland by a pressure-driven flow. It has been shown, using pH-sensitive dyes, that when acid is secreted, a jet of acid pushes through the mucus layer in narrow channels, and this "viscous fingering" allows the acid to reach the lumen without mixing and being neutralised by the bicarbonate in the surface mucus. The mucus layer thus retains the neutral pH at the epithelial surface and the low pH in the lumen, as a pH gradient across the mucus.

The parietal cell also protects itself: its apical membrane, facing the canaliculus, is specialised and resistant to acid, and the cell pumps out H+ via the H+/K+ ATPase while maintaining its intracellular pH.

answer:
A stress fracture is a small crack or a region of bone damage, caused by repetitive loading that exceeds the bone's capacity to repair itself, as opposed to a single large force. It's not a hairline crack through the entire bone, in most cases, and it often begins as microdamage and a local reaction in the bone.

When you run, the bone is subjected to repeated loads, which cause microscopic damage. Normally, the bone remodels in response, with osteoclasts removing damaged bone and osteoblasts laying down new bone. If the loading continues without enough time to repair, the damage accumulates faster than it can be repaired, and the area becomes weak. The process gradually progresses from stress reaction, with bone marrow oedema and periosteal reaction, to a true fracture line in the cortex, which is a thin crack in the outer layer. So the lesion in the early stage is more of a remodelling problem than a visible break.

That is why X-rays often don't show stress fractures at first. X-rays show bone density and structure, and they depend on there being a visible crack or a change in bone mineral density, or new bone formation on the surface, which takes two to three weeks, and sometimes more than that, to become evident. In the early phase, there may be no change in the structure of the bone that is visible. The sensitivity of plain X-rays for early stress fractures is quite low, perhaps 15 to 35 percent.

MRI can detect the changes in the bone marrow and the surrounding soft tissue, which are not visible on X-rays. The oedema, which is increased water content due to inflammation and the repair response, shows up brightly on fluid-sensitive sequences, and MRI can detect a stress reaction within days, with a sensitivity near 100 percent. What you see on the MRI is, therefore, the bone's reaction to the injury, along with the fracture line in more advanced cases.

There has been research in this area, but so far no alternative treatment has been shown to reliably cure rabies once symptoms appear, and the standard approach remains post-exposure prophylaxis before symptoms start.

The Milwaukee protocol, first used in 2004 on Jeanna Giese, involved placing the patient in a medically induced coma and giving antiviral drugs, with the idea of protecting the brain while the immune system produced antibodies. It was thought that rabies might damage the brain in a functional way, rather than by killing neurons, and that supportive care might allow recovery. Jeanna Giese survived, but later attempts to replicate the protocol have had a very low success rate, and a number of reviews concluded that the survivors may have had a milder form of disease or had received some prior immunity or vaccination. The protocol is no longer recommended as a standard treatment.

As for injecting antivirals directly into the brain, this has been considered in principle, and intrathecal administration of drugs, such as antibodies, has been tried in some cases without a clear benefit. The main obstacles are that by the time symptoms occur, the virus has already infected widespread areas of the nervous system, and rabies spreads along the neurons, within cells, where antibodies and many drugs don't reach it easily. In addition, none of the antivirals tested, such as ribavirin, favipiravir, and amantadine, have shown efficacy in rabies.

Research continues on monoclonal antibodies, new antivirals, and combination therapies, but for now, prevention is the key. Prompt washing of the wound and vaccination, with rabies immune globulin, is nearly 100 percent effective if started before symptoms.

answer:
No, a disease doesn't need a known cause to be called a disease, and the Dorland's definition you quote is the more accurate and widely used one. The distinction between a disease and a syndrome depends on whether there is a unified, defined pathological process, not just on whether the cause is known.

A disease is generally considered to be a particular abnormal condition with a characteristic set of signs and symptoms, and often a recognised pathology or course. As Dorland's says, the etiology, pathology, and prognosis may be known or unknown. For example, many conditions were recognised as diseases long before their causes were understood, such as multiple sclerosis, schizophrenia, rheumatoid arthritis, and Crohn's disease, and some still have uncertain causes. These are clearly treated as diseases.

A syndrome is a collection of signs and symptoms that tend to occur together, which may have multiple possible causes, and it may or may not be a distinct disease. For example, "nephrotic syndrome" can result from many different kidney diseases, and "irritable bowel syndrome" is a collection of symptoms without a single known pathology. Some syndromes are later found to have a single cause, and then they are sometimes reclassified, or renamed as diseases, such as "AIDS", which is the syndrome caused by HIV infection, and Down syndrome, which is caused by trisomy 21, though the name remains a syndrome for historical reasons.

So the usage is not entirely consistent, and the terms overlap. In practice, the names often follow history and convention, and they don't reflect a rigorous classification.

answer: When you breathe out and back in, you replace the gas in your lungs with the gas in the outside air. The lungs have a high surface area interface between blood gas and lung gas and function to make the partial pressures of gases in the lungs and blood nearly equal. Importantly, you do not use up all the oxygen in the lungs between breaths. To do so, you'd have to also use up all the oxygen in the blood: remember that the lungs make the partial pressures nearly equal. Typical partial pressures of oxygen in the atmosphere are around 160 Torr, lungs around 100 Torr, arterial blood around 100 Torr, venous blood around 50 Torr. See for example Wikipedia Pulmonary Gas Pressures . If you hold your breath, then the total oxygen in your body is the amount dissolved in the blood and all the tissues and the amount in the lungs. You'll eventually use this up in metabolism, and when the partial pressure of oxygen drops sufficiently you will eventually lose consciousness, but this is relatively slow. If you breathe an inert gas like nitrogen, every breath is a pump taking the amount of oxygen in the lungs and replacing it with zero oxygen. The lungs then will fill with some oxygen from the blood before the next breath, at which point it will all be pumped out again.

question_context: Wikipedia says that inhaling a pure inert gas causes a loss of consciousness in only a few breaths. But how can that be if people can hold their breath for way longer, well over a minute or even two minutes, without becoming unconscious? Does the extra air your breath in during the "deep breath" contain enough oxygen to account for this?
label: ai

answer:
The main reason is that the urge to breathe and the loss of consciousness depend on different signals, and inert gas asphyxiation takes advantage of the difference. The comparison with breath-holding is misleading, because they are physiologically different situations.

When you hold your breath, you keep the oxygen that is already in your lungs and blood, and carbon dioxide gradually builds up. The strong urge to breathe is driven primarily by rising CO2 levels, not falling oxygen, and so most people break their breath-hold after one to two minutes, long before they lose consciousness from low oxygen. Even if you do hold your breath for a long time, the blood oxygen level declines slowly and the lungs contain enough oxygen to maintain it for a while. Typical breath-holds are ended by the CO2 drive, and the oxygen is only just dropping to low levels, so you remain conscious. Free divers who hyperventilate beforehand to lower CO2 can black out because their urge to breathe is suppressed.

With inert gas inhalation, such as nitrogen or helium, you continue to breathe normally. Each breath washes oxygen out of the lungs, and the gas you take in contains none, so the alveolar oxygen falls rapidly toward zero within a few breaths. Meanwhile, the CO2 is still removed from the blood with each exhalation, so CO2 levels don't rise, and you don't feel the air hunger or panic that would normally signal that something is wrong. The oxygen concentration in the blood drops sharply, because the lungs no longer hold any reserve, and the oxygen in the blood is flushed out as it passes through the lungs and diffuses back into the alveoli. Consciousness is lost within about 15 to 20 seconds, and sometimes with no warning.

So breath-holding keeps your oxygen reserve in the lungs, while inert gas breathing actively removes it.

question: Can daily bike commuting reduce male fertility?
question_context: Does commuting to school or work every day by bike reduce male fertility? Say, 25 minutes each way, for a total of 50 minutes every weekday. I have heard this is a known issue among people who ride a lot, but the question is whether what I described above counts as “a lot”. Of course, fertility naturally declines over the years, but I mean the additional effect that might result from cycling to work — the “delta” on top of the natural process. Alternative options could be by car (also sitting, but without leg movement) or walking. I weigh 60 kg and live a healthy life style - no smoking, drinking, good nutrition.
label: human

answer: Normal recreational cycling is not generally considered a major cause of male infertility. Very high-volume cycling, prolonged heat exposure, pressure from the saddle, intense training, or associated hormonal and energy-balance changes might affect semen parameters in some men. Evidence is mixed, and effects are not necessarily permanent. If fertility is a concern, adjusting training load and bike fit and obtaining a medical evaluation is more useful than assuming commuting itself is harmful.

answer:
The evidence suggests that moderate commuting by bicycle of the type you describe is unlikely to cause a meaningful reduction in male fertility, though research is limited, and the findings are mixed.

The concerns about cycling and fertility relate to three possible mechanisms. The first is scrotal heat. Prolonged sitting and tight clothing raise scrotal temperature, which can impair sperm production, because the testes work best a degree or two below core body temperature. The second is pressure and trauma to the perineum from the saddle, which may affect blood flow or cause microtrauma. The third is hormonal and physiological stress from very intense training.

The studies that have found negative effects mostly involve competitive or high-volume cyclists, such as those riding several hundred kilometres per week. For example, some studies of triathletes and cyclists have reported lower sperm concentration or motility, or a higher proportion of abnormal sperm morphology, compared with non-cyclists, though other studies have not found significant differences, and the effects are often modest. A study of men who cycled more than about 5 hours per week found lower sperm concentration, but those at less than 5 hours showed little difference. Your 50 minutes a day, about 4 hours per week, is below that range, and commuting is typically at a lower intensity than training.

Practical steps that may help are using a well-fitted saddle, perhaps one with a cut-out or a wider design, wearing loose clothing, standing on the pedals now and then, and taking breaks. Cycling also provides cardiovascular and general health benefits, which are linked to better fertility. If you are trying to conceive and have concerns, a semen analysis is the most direct way to check, and you can compare results over time.

answer: There is no "rigorous science" behind the claim. Whether Tylenol/acetaminophen (N- a cetyl- p ara- a mino p henol/APAP) causes autism has been looked at in many studies, but there has not been any solid evidence to date that it does , while the opposite, that APAP does not cause autism, has been borne out in some good studies. There are a number of studies that show APAP use may contribute to "neurodevelopmental problems" (ADHD and other conditions) later in life, but the vast majority of studies are flawed. First, they mostly rely on memory/self reporting, which is notoriously problematic. Another is that the reason women might take APAP during pregnancy, e.g. for fever, pain, or conditions which are painful (e.g. arthritis/other inflammatory conditions) may be the causative factor itself, as opposed to the pain meds. Again, this is a very difficult confounding factor. Another issue is the genetics of autism. What we do know about autism is that there is a strong genetic component; studies are starting to locate genes associated with (?responsible for) the condition. Studies of twins and siblings have shown that the incidence of autism spectrum disorder in identical twins is as high as 90%, and in siblings, either dizygotic twins or separate pregnancies, it's as high as 30%. Autism is also somewhat dependent on environmental factors, e.g. the family the child is born into and the exposures it may have. That's another problem with most of the studies; it's difficult to determine the association of autism with medication use because subjects and controls are raised in different environments which cannot be controlled for. So, unless the controls are raised in the same environment (impossible for non-sibling controls), the causation cannot be proven for APAP use. The largest and best study, was published last year in the Journal of the American Medical Association. It is a Swedish study with over 2.4 million children. The study attempted to compensate for the lack of controls most studies are plagued with by using sibling-matched controls, and found no evidence of increased incidence of autism with APAP use. There is a higher incidence of autism in circumcised males, but is that because of the pain associated with the procedure or with the analgesic administered for post-surgical pain? That's not a minor point. All types of pain in neonates, especially preemies, is associated with a higher incidence of neurodevelopmental disorders. The use of analgesics in such cases is ubiquitous. Which factor caused what? Corellation does not equal causation. To do a proper study, one would need to have a group of boys get post-circumcision APAP, and another group to be denied APAP, or to receive a more dangerous analgesic or local anesthesia/nerve block, and follow those infants for 10 years. However, any use of APAP during infancy for any reason would would confound the results.
question: Is there any credibility to the USA department of Health claim that tylenol causes autism?
question_context: We have all heard the recent claim by the USA department of health that tylenol (acetaminophen) is a risk factor for autism. Ostensibly this claim comes from an examination of scholarly research linking circumcision of babies to a high risk of developing autism with pain being seen as a likely cause. The USA department of health looked into pain control methods used and discovered that against expectations babies given acetaminophen had a notably higher risk than those given no pain control. Does this constiute rigorus sceince?
label: human

answer: Claims that acetaminophen directly causes autism are not established by high-quality evidence. Some observational studies have reported associations between prenatal acetaminophen use and later neurodevelopmental outcomes, but those studies are vulnerable to confounding by the illness, fever, genetics, and other factors that led to medication use. An association does not prove causation. Pregnant patients should discuss medication use with their clinician rather than stopping necessary treatment based on headlines.

Does this constiute rigorus sceince?

answer:
There's no strong evidence that supports a causal link between acetaminophen and autism, and in general, the scientific consensus is that the evidence doesn't justify such a claim. The recent statements have been criticised by many medical and scientific organisations.

The claim's basis is mostly observational studies, which have found an association between acetaminophen use during pregnancy or early childhood and a slightly higher risk of autism or ADHD in some groups. But observational studies can't establish causation, because they are subject to confounding. The reasons that mothers or children take acetaminophen, such as fever, infection, pain, or inflammation, may themselves be linked to autism risk, and genetic factors that influence both the condition being treated and the child's neurodevelopment can also play a role. Maternal fever during pregnancy has been associated with autism, and untreated fever may be harmful, so that avoiding acetaminophen could be worse.

The strongest evidence on the question came from a large Swedish sibling-comparison study published in JAMA in 2024, which compared siblings who were exposed and not exposed to acetaminophen during pregnancy. It found that the association disappeared when family factors were controlled for, which suggests that the link in other studies is due to confounding. Sibling comparisons are a better design for controlling shared genetics and environment.

In the circumcision-related claim you mention, the same issues apply, and the reasoning that pain causes autism and that acetaminophen worsens it is speculative. There is also no robust evidence for the idea that circumcision pain causes autism.

So, this doesn't constitute rigorous science. Organisations such as the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the European Medicines Agency, have said that acetaminophen remains an appropriate option when needed during pregnancy, at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time. Anyone concerned about their use should talk to their doctor.

question: Can a muscle issue like a pull or knot, irritate a nerve and cause atrophy in connected muscles?
question_context: I understand that things like bone spurs or bulging disks in the spine can impinge on the nerve roots and cause neurological symptoms like pain and loss of sensation or muscle strength, in body areas that correspond to the nerve root. This is called radiculopathy . I'm interested in learning whether muscular conditions, further from the spine, might cause similar symptoms. For example, can a pulled muscle , or a muscle "knot" (aka myofascial trigger points ), also irritate a nerve and trigger significant muscle strength loss from interrupted nerve signals? I'm imagining this irritation would occur not at the spinal root, but somewhere where the nerve branch is still large, like in the brachial plexus or arm pit area (for upper body symptoms). One issue I'm having, as I try to research this topic online, is that a topic like muscle knots leads to concepts and treatments that range from science-based, to speculative, to quackery.
label: human

answer: A muscle injury can irritate or compress a nearby nerve in some situations, especially if swelling, altered movement, or scar tissue affects the nerve. However, true muscle atrophy in muscles supplied by that nerve can also signal a more significant nerve injury or other neurological problem. Persistent weakness, numbness, visible wasting, or progressive symptoms should be medically evaluated rather than attributed to a simple knot or strain.

answer:
Yes, in principle, and a nerve can be irritated or compressed by muscles or other soft tissues along its path, which is called a peripheral nerve entrapment. But true atrophy from a simple muscle pull or knot is uncommon, and it generally requires significant and sustained nerve compression or injury.

Peripheral nerves run through and between muscles and fascia, and in certain places they pass through tight spaces. Muscles that are tight, hypertrophied, or in spasm can compress a nerve at these sites, and examples are well recognised. Piriformis syndrome is where the piriformis muscle in the buttock may compress the sciatic nerve. Thoracic outlet syndrome involves compression of the brachial plexus by neck muscles such as the scalenes. Pronator syndrome is where the median nerve is compressed by the pronator teres muscle in the forearm. Other examples include the entrapment of the radial nerve at the supinator (radial tunnel syndrome) and the suprascapular nerve.

These conditions typically cause pain, numbness, tingling, or weakness in the area supplied by the nerve. When compression is mild, it causes a temporary conduction block (neurapraxia), which leads to weakness but not atrophy. For atrophy to occur, there has to be axonal damage, which interrupts the nerve's connection to the muscle for weeks or months, causing denervation. That is more likely with severe or prolonged compression, or a direct injury, such as a tear or contusion.

Myofascial trigger points are thought to cause local and referred pain, but there is limited evidence that they directly cause denervation or atrophy. The weakness that comes with pain is often due to inhibition from pain and disuse, not true nerve damage. Disuse itself can cause some atrophy over time.

If you have progressive weakness, muscle wasting, or numbness, you should see a doctor, who may arrange nerve conduction studies and an EMG to find out what is going on.

answer: Overview of Cancer All nucleated cells in the body have means of proliferation (by proto-oncogenes ) and deliberate self-induced death (by tumor suppressors ), which they regulate according to their functions; for example, a cell in the lining of the esophagus proliferates rapidly, while neurons have typically all but ceased their proliferation in adulthood. When genes that induce cell death and prevent proliferation, or the products of those genes, are altered (for instance due to a mutation), there's a likelihood that the cell may enter an endless cycle of proliferation. This is a cell in its so-called precancerous state that can quickly, or slowly, become fully cancerous. A real-life example is p53 , a tumor suppressor protein, loss of whose function, often due to a mutation in the gene encoding it, is implicated in the pathology of half of all known cancers [1]. Once a cell is cancerous, unless identified and removed by the immune system, which happens in >99% of the cases, it deviates more and more from normal ones as the cancer progresses. It will cease to perform normal tissue function, and instead devote all the resources it can muster to an increasingly faulty mitosis. In doing so, it will utilize many cellular pathways involved in signaling the cell to proliferate. A series of these pathways involve remodeling tissue structure, something our body normally does constantly in response to the shear and tear that frequently happens in epithelia across the body. SERPINB3, a Biomarker of Cancer The principle guiding diagnosis and treatment, whether of cancer or skin warts, is to target molecules and processes the disruption of which would cause minimal damage to healthy cells while effectively removing the undesired ones. If you do achieve this ideal, you will have cured that cancer type. To diagnose a certain type of cancer, a circulating molecule was found to be sensitive and specific, and thus a suitable biomarker, and after a few name changes, was named SERPINB3 [2,3]. SERPINB3 is a serine proteinase inhibitor involved in tissue remodeling, among its other roles [2]. In simple terms, if the linings of the tissues in the body are some sort of fabric, the body uses other fabric, tailor's knives, scissors, and sheaths to shape the fabric in specific ways. SERPINB3 is a sheath. Cancerous cells employ the body's "tailoring tools", including SERPINB3, to remodel the tissue so they would take up more space and invade lymph nodes. The levels of SERPINB3 in circulation thus increase in certain cancer types, enabling (early) diagnosis to guide clinical decisions forward. SERPINB3 in Wound Healing Process To sum up the previous section, what happened, chronologically, is that the levels of a certain protein in the blood were found to have been increased in a certain cancer type, suggesting that tracking its levels was a useful way of diagnosing that cancer type. Since then, this target has been found to be a useful diagnostic marker in several other cancers as well. Its gene was described, and several roles for it had been identified. The main role for SERPINB3 in the body had been elusive, however, and that's what's been the focus of the new study by Yaron et al. After harmful debris left by a wound is cleaned up by the immune system, re-epithelization is the process during which new epithelium restores tissue integrity in the skin [4]. It is initiated by the activation and migration of keratinocytes to the site of the wound, and the authors propose that SERPINB3 plays a pivotal role in stimulating this process. As has been explained above, the role of SERPINB3 in re-epithelization is not incongruous with its role in cancer. SERPINB3, in healthy tissue as well as cancerous ones, acts as a cog in the complex machinery involved in remodeling and modifying tissue. Whether targeting it to enhance the wound healing process in various disease states such as chronic ulcers would be viable is not a question the study answers, and further research is needed to explore such possibilities, which would depend on a myriad of factors pertinent to the feasibility of any such endeavor, which are too broad to delve into in an answer here. answer: SerpinB3 is a member of the serpin family of protease inhibitors. It is expressed particularly in squamous epithelial tissues and is thought to help regulate protease activity, inflammation, and cellular responses to stress or injury. Its expression can increase in some cancers and inflammatory conditions, which is why it has been studied as a biomarker. Its normal physiological roles are still being investigated and are likely context-dependent.

answer:
Prophylactic intubation is considered in spinal cord injury, but it's not automatic, and the decision depends on the level of injury and the patient's respiratory status. In the question you describe, the clues usually point to a high cervical injury where respiratory function is likely to decline.

The respiratory muscles are controlled by different levels of the cord. The diaphragm is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5), and the intercostal muscles by thoracic nerves. A patient with a cervical injury at C5 or above may initially have an acceptable respiratory rate and oxygen level, but they can deteriorate over the first hours to days. There are a number of reasons: ascending oedema and swelling in the cord, which may extend the level of injury upward, fatigue from the work of breathing with a weak chest wall, and aspiration. In addition, the loss of intercostal muscle function reduces vital capacity.

A patient who has quadriplegia, as in your example, with a respiratory rate of 14, may look stable, but if there are signs such as paradoxical (abdominal) breathing, a falling vital capacity (below about 15 mL/kg), or a falling oxygen saturation, early intubation is recommended. In many exam questions, the intended answer is to secure the airway early with intubation, because the patient is at risk of respiratory failure, using in-line cervical stabilisation and, typically, an approach like fibre-optic or video laryngoscopy to avoid neck movement. Succinylcholine is generally avoided after the first 48 hours, due to the risk of hyperkalaemia, but it's acceptable in the acute period.

So the answer depends on the details in the question.

In medicine, a pathogen is typically defined as any agent that can cause disease in a host. The definition doesn't depend on being alive or on having its own genome. Viruses are often described as non-living or borderline, since they can't reproduce outside a host cell, and they are still universally regarded as pathogens. Prions are infectious proteins that propagate by causing normal host prion protein to misfold, and since they can be transmitted between individuals and cause disease, they meet the definition of a pathogen. They are also listed as pathogens in infectious disease classifications, and the prion diseases are regarded as transmissible spongiform encephalopathies.

There are other terms that people use, including "infectious agent," "infectious particle," or "proteinaceous infectious particle," from which the word prion was derived by Stanley Prusiner. The term "infectious agent" is perhaps the most inclusive, as it covers bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites, and prions. Some also use "transmissible agent."

One nuance is that prions can also arise spontaneously or through genetic mutation without any external exposure, as in sporadic and familial Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, so in these cases, there is no transmission from another individual.

In sum, you can call prions pathogens, and there's no need for a different blanket term, though "infectious agent" is a good general-purpose alternative.

answer:
The difference is most likely due to how the two sequences handle imperfections, such as the refocusing pulses, diffusion, and, most importantly, stimulated and indirect echoes in a multi-slice spin-echo sequence, and not because the water itself has a different T2.

Distilled water has a very long T2, on the order of seconds, and your CPMG result of 1,200 to 1,300 ms is plausible, though it can be limited by diffusion in field gradients, and by imperfect refocusing pulses. The T2mapMSME is a multi-slice multi-echo (MSME) sequence, and its results are typically shorter for long T2 samples, for several reasons.

First, in MSME, the slice-selective refocusing pulses are not perfect 180 degree pulses because of the slice profile and B1 inhomogeneity, so the signal includes stimulated and indirect echo pathways, which can bias the estimated T2. Second, the crusher gradients around the refocusing pulses make the signal sensitive to diffusion, and for water, which has a high diffusion coefficient, this adds an attenuation that shortens the apparent T2, particularly with long echo spacing. A CPMG with a short echo spacing minimises this effect. Third, the number of echoes and the echo spacing in the MSME sequence may not allow the signal to decay sufficiently for accurate fitting of a long T2, especially if the last echo time is much shorter than 3 to 5 times the T2. If the echo train covers only a fraction of the decay, the fit is poor. Fourth, the fitting model matters. A mono-exponential fit that does not include the first echo, or fitting to a noise floor, can bias the results.

To compare them properly, use the same echo spacing, a longer echo train, check the pulse calibration, and consider a fit that accounts for stimulated echoes. The Bruker T2mapMSME also offers an option for fitting with or without the first echo.

The evidence base for St John's Wort in anxiety is much weaker than for depression, and your summary is broadly accurate, with a few additional points to consider.

NICE guidance, including CG113 on generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder and CG159 on social anxiety, doesn't recommend St John's Wort for anxiety, and it says to warn people about the risks of using it. This is because of the lack of good evidence of benefit and the safety concerns about interactions. Both guidelines also note the uncertainty about dose and the variability in preparations.

The clinical studies that exist are small and of low to moderate quality. Some trials, such as an early study by Kobak and colleagues in social anxiety, found no benefit over placebo, and a trial in GAD found some symptomatic improvement, but the sample sizes and methodology limit the conclusions. A study by Sarris and colleagues on herbal treatments for anxiety, and subsequent systematic reviews, concluded that the evidence is inconsistent and that any benefit may be related to its antidepressant effect in people with comorbid depressive symptoms, rather than to a specific anxiolytic effect. The mechanism, which involves inhibition of reuptake of serotonin, noradrenaline, and dopamine, mostly attributed to hyperforin, makes it plausible but unproven.

You're right about the safety issues. St John's Wort is a potent inducer of CYP3A4, CYP2C9, and P-glycoprotein, which reduces the levels of many drugs, including oral contraceptives, anticoagulants such as warfarin, immunosuppressants such as ciclosporin, some antiretrovirals, and others, and it can cause serotonin syndrome when combined with SSRIs. The BNF carries these warnings. Under the UK's traditional herbal registration scheme, THR products are authorised for low mood and mild anxiety on the basis of traditional use and not clinical trials, which is why you may see it labelled for "mild anxiety" despite the lack of evidence.

So, for primary anxiety, it shouldn't be recommended, and the pharmacist's role is mainly counselling about interactions and directing patients to evidence-based options such as CBT and SSRIs.

answer:
No, the smear test has no established clinical value as a way to confirm or exclude melena, and spreading the stool to look for a reddish colour is not a recognised diagnostic method. Your understanding of melena is correct.

Melena is black, tarry, foul-smelling stool resulting from the digestion of blood, usually from an upper GI source such as the stomach or duodenum, and sometimes from the small bowel or right colon. The blood is altered by gastric acid and bacterial action, which turns haemoglobin into haematin, giving it the black colour and sticky texture. It's the chemical change, and not the amount of unaltered red blood, that determines the colour, so there is nothing particularly red to see when you smear it. It may sometimes show a brownish-red tint when spread thinly, but its absence doesn't rule it out, and its presence doesn't confirm it.

The proper way to distinguish melena from other causes of dark stool is by clinical features and, when needed, by testing. The consistency and odour are characteristic, and stool that is black, sticky, and foul-smelling, particularly in a patient with risk factors such as NSAID use, ulcers, or liver disease, makes melena likely. A faecal occult blood test, or a rectal examination with a guaiac test, can detect the presence of blood, though false positives and negatives occur. Other causes of black stool include iron supplements, bismuth (such as Pepto-Bismol), activated charcoal, and certain foods, such as black liquorice or blueberries, and these stools are usually dark green-black, formed, and not tarry, and they test negative for blood.

If melena is suspected, the next steps are assessing haemodynamic stability, checking haemoglobin and urea, and arranging an upper endoscopy. Dismissing melena only on the basis of a smear test could delay important diagnosis.

answer: This is a very interesting question! The most critical difference between a male and female heart is the size and ventricular load. Although the physiological characteristics of a heart can and do adapt to the donor's body, there are certainly limitations to this function. Prior to modern predictions of left-ventricular mass using imaging technology, opposite-sex transplants often lead to heart failure. For female hearts being transplanted to a male's body, any significant size difference (which is relatively common due to the 25%~ lower average size of the female heart) could lead to overstretching of cardiomyocytes in the heart due to the higher blood volume per stroke necessary in a male cardiovascular system. "..compared to the male heart, the female heart has a larger ejection fraction and beats at a faster rate but generates a smaller cardiac output." (ref1) The gendered electrophysiology of the heart is primarily dependent on hormonal signaling. As this suggests, testosterone production will cause the electrophysiology of the heart to adapt. "The female and male hearts do not only differ in mass and size but also display a myriad of functional, structural, genetic, and hormonal differences: women have a higher resting heart rate than men, but their hearts take a long time from contraction to relaxation. This is a result of the action of testosterone during ventricular repolarization... ...and we can observe it through longer QT intervals in the electrocardiogram." (ref1) Long-term, testosterone also stimulates the hypertrophy of cardiomyocytes in the heart, which is another example of gender-based adaptation. Within heart transplantation itself, response to exercise and/or stress can be weakened due to denervation of the transplant to the receiver, which lengthens the response time of the nervous system to increasing the beating rate of the heart. This is usually temporary and reinnervation occurs long-term after transplantation. This process is not necessarily gender-specific. "Since cardiac transplant patients have denervated hearts, they provide a unique model for isolating central versus peripheral influences on the cardiovascular response to stress.. ..heart rate increase during the mental arithmetic task was significantly attenuated in the transplant recipients." (ref2) In short, yes, both short-term and long-term physiological adaptation is likely, and the most important factor to determining opposite-sex transplantation success is a size-match to prevent myocardial overload that can lead to heart failure. (It's also necessary to mention immunological rejection, but assumedly there is (concurrently) not a significant difference in treatment of this kind of transplant rejection compared to sex-matched transplantations, though complications relating to rejection are more likely. question: Does a transplanted woman's heart function differently in a man?
question_context: Suppose a man receives a successful heart transplant from a woman. After the transplant, would the heart function exactly the same way as it did in the female donor, or could its function change because it is now inside a male body? For example, could the recipient's sex affect the heart's heart rate, contraction strength, electrical activity, or response to exercise? answer: A transplanted heart does not fundamentally change its biological function based on whether the recipient is male or female. The donor heart retains the donor's chromosomes, but its rate, workload, and remodeling adapt to the recipient's body size, hormones, blood pressure, medications, and activity. Sex mismatch can influence transplant outcomes in some studies, partly through size and immune factors, but the heart does not simply become a “male” or “female” heart after transplantation.

answer:
In general, a transplanted heart keeps functioning as a heart, and the donor's sex doesn't prevent it from working in a recipient of the opposite sex, but there are some differences that can matter, and the heart does adapt to some extent.

Immediately after transplant, the donor heart is denervated, meaning its nerve connections to the recipient's autonomic nervous system have been cut. This leads to a higher resting heart rate, usually 90 to 110 beats per minute, and a delayed response to exercise, since it depends on circulating adrenaline, and not direct nerve signals. This is independent of the sex of the donor, and some reinnervation may occur over years.

Size is the more important factor. Women's hearts are on average smaller than men's, with a smaller left ventricular mass and cavity. A heart from a small female donor may be too small for a larger male recipient, because it may not provide adequate cardiac output, and so transplant teams match donors and recipients by body size and use predicted heart mass. Studies suggest that female-to-male transplants, particularly with a size mismatch, have somewhat worse outcomes, which has been observed in registry data, and the cause is likely multifactorial.

Intrinsic characteristics of the heart muscle cells, such as electrical properties and the sensitivity to hormones, may differ between sexes, since sex chromosomes and sex hormones influence heart function. For example, women's hearts tend to have a longer QT interval. The cells in the donor heart still carry the donor's genes, so some of those traits may persist. The recipient's hormones, though, will affect the heart, and the transplanted heart may adapt in terms of size, with some hypertrophy occurring in response to the recipient's higher demand.

So the heart will retain many of its intrinsic properties, but it will also be influenced by its new environment, and the matching process is meant to minimise problems.

answer:
The vertical incision in an emergency airway procedure, such as a cricothyrotomy, is used because of the anatomy of the neck, and the choice of a vertical or horizontal incision depends on the setting and the surgeon's training.

In an emergency cricothyrotomy, the target is the cricothyroid membrane, a thin membrane between the thyroid cartilage and the cricoid cartilage, located in the midline of the neck. In a patient who can't be intubated or ventilated, the quickest way to establish an airway is to cut through this membrane. The vertical skin incision, typically 3 to 4 cm in the midline, is preferred in emergencies where the landmarks can't be felt, because it allows the operator to extend the incision upwards or downwards to find the membrane, and it avoids the blood vessels. The main vessels in the neck, the anterior jugular veins, run vertically on either side of the midline, so a vertical midline incision tends to avoid them, whereas a horizontal incision could cut across them and cause heavy bleeding. Moreover, if the surgeon misjudges the position, a vertical incision can be extended without having to start over.

Once the skin is incised, and the membrane is identified, a horizontal incision is made through the cricothyroid membrane itself, and the tube is inserted. So the cut in the membrane is horizontal, while the skin incision is vertical.

In a planned, non-emergency tracheostomy, surgeons often use a horizontal skin incision, as it provides a better cosmetic result, and the landmarks are easier to identify. That's what you see in the case of a controlled operating room setting. Modern emergency practice also includes the scalpel-bougie-tube technique, which uses a horizontal stab incision through the membrane after palpating the landmarks, and a vertical skin incision only if the landmarks aren't palpable.

It means that flight arose independently in three separate vertebrate lineages: pterosaurs, birds, and bats. Each of those groups descends from a flightless ancestor, and their last common ancestor with the others couldn't fly either. That's why wings in these groups are analogous rather than homologous. The forelimb is the shared starting point, but the wing structure differs. A pterosaur wing is a membrane supported by one hugely elongated finger, a bat wing is a membrane stretched across several elongated fingers, and a bird wing is built from feathers attached to the arm and hand.

Your second reading is partly right, but it's not what the phrase claims. The statement is about the minimum number of origins, not a claim that each group started from a single species. Within a lineage, the ancestral population that evolved flight would have been a population, and its descendants would later diversify. Whether flight arose more than once inside a group is a separate question. For bats and pterosaurs there is no good evidence for it, and the fossil and molecular data point to one origin each. For birds the picture is more debated because many feathered, wing-bearing dinosaurs like Microraptor and Anchiornis may have had some gliding or flapping ability, so powered flight may have evolved more than once within the broader bird-line theropods. The "three times" figure is the conservative, widely accepted count.

Insects are usually left out of the phrase only because it says vertebrates.

The house mouse and its relatives are used in research mazes like the Morris water maze, which depends on mice swimming for an extended period to find an escape platform. In those tests, healthy lab mice typically swim for minutes at a stretch without sinking, using a paddling gait with their hind legs and with their tail serving as a rudder.

A fall from 50 cm into room-temperature water would startle a mouse, but it would very probably surface and swim. Swimming three metres is well within normal ability, and it should take perhaps ten seconds or so, since mice swim at roughly 0.2 to 0.3 m/s. The caveat is that endurance is limited by cooling. Mice are small with a high surface-area-to-volume ratio, so they lose heat quickly in water, and in cold water they would tire and become hypothermic within a relatively short time. In the forced swim test, mice are generally removed after about six minutes to avoid exhaustion.

So for your scenario the answer is yes, with essentially no trouble. A wild house mouse in a pond would also manage, though it would struggle to climb out of a smooth-sided container.

Not in the standard sense, and there are good reasons why. The premeiotic S phase is what makes the two rounds of division possible. After replication, each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids. Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes, and meiosis II separates the sister chromatids. If DNA is not replicated, meiosis I would still separate the homologs and give two haploid cells, but each chromosome would be a single chromatid, and there would be no way for a second division to produce further viable cells without another round of replication.

The real question then is whether a single division without replication could work, and the answer is that it is mechanistically possible but not observed as a normal pathway in diploid organisms. Recombination, which happens during meiotic prophase I, depends on having sister chromatids to repair double-strand breaks and form crossovers with the homologs, and crossovers are required in most species to hold homologs together so they segregate correctly. Skipping replication would undermine this.

There are some odd exceptions in nature, such as meiotic variants in parthenogenetic species that include premeiotic doubling or endoreduplication, but these still involve replication. Mutants in yeast and other organisms that bypass S phase before meiotic divisions generally produce inviable gametes.

Over a full cycle, the pile commonly loses 30 to 50 percent of its dry organic matter, plus a great deal of water through evaporation, so the assumption becomes poor. Because the evaporation term is already in the balance (through the enthalpy difference of the airflow), some of the water loss is accounted for. But treating mc as constant means that the thermal inertia of the pile is overestimated late in the process, which usually shows up as predicted temperatures lagging behind measured ones during cooling.

More realistic models write the mass as a function of time, with separate terms for dry matter, water, and sometimes air, and compute an effective heat capacity as a mass-weighted sum.

Your intuition about the timescale is a good one to examine, but 40,000 years is more than enough for large morphological change when selection is strong and deliberate. A few things help to reconcile this.

First, the extreme variety you see in modern breeds is very recent. Most breeds were created in the last few hundred years, mostly in the last 200, through intense artificial selection. Dogs from earlier periods were far more uniform and wolf-like. So the wide spread between a Chihuahua and a Great Dane developed over a few centuries, not 40,000 years.

Second, artificial selection is much faster than natural selection. When humans choose which individuals breed, with generations every one to two years, strong selection on traits like size or snout length produces rapid change. The famous Russian fox experiment produced tame, floppy-eared, piebald foxes within only a few decades.

Third, dog size and shape are strongly influenced by a small number of genes of large effect. For example, a single variant in the IGF1 gene accounts for much of the size difference between small and large breeds. This means big differences can come from relatively few mutations, and a lot of variation was already present in ancestral wolf populations.

Also note that the exact timing of domestication is debated, with estimates ranging from 15,000 to 40,000 years or more.

answer: I think you have your information a bit twisted here. Influenza virus in humans is still an airborne virus, the problem is that the virus doesn't transmit well between humans because of problems with the virus itself - usually the form of the hemagglutinin (HA) on the viral surface, which binds to sialic acids on the lung epithelium. In humans the sialic acids in the upper airway are predominantly α2,6-linked, while in the lower airway (i.e. deep in the lungs) they are predominantly α2,3-linked forms. Deep lung infections are difficult to transmit because it is hard to get the aerosols out of the lungs. So, virus forms with HA that bind α2,3-linked sialic acids won't transmit well between humans. It also means that viruses of this form can't easily infect humans as they generally need to get deep into the lung to do so. However, avian species, which are the majority of natural hosts for influenzas have it the other way around - they have α2,3-linked sialic acids at the surfaces where transmission is easiest. This is usually the gut in birds, rather than the lungs, but the mechanism of viral attachment and aerosol spread hold true for both birds and humans. So, there is a barrier between humans and avian species in terms of viruses they put out and how they infect. This isn't to say that influenzas that bind best to α2,3-linked sialic acids won't infect humans at all, they certainly can do so and will given the opportunity, but they generate an infection that doesn't transmit well human-to-human. Rob Mettelman and Paul Thomas wrote a freely available review of influenza infectivity in humans titled " Human Susceptibility to Influenza Infection and Severe Disease " 1 , if you need more information. question: What does a virus need to transmit through air between humans?
question_context: For now, the avian flu outbreak is said to stop short of a human pandemic because human-to-human transmission has not been observed. However, people are getting sick from contact with infected animals, and coughing is one of the symptoms. What factors could be preventing airborne transmission, and how would the virus need to change to accomplish it?
label: human

answer: For a virus to transmit efficiently through air between humans, several things must line up. It must be released from an infected person in respiratory particles, remain infectious long enough outside the body, reach another person's respiratory tract, and infect cells at the new site. Particle size matters because smaller aerosols can remain suspended longer, while larger droplets settle more quickly. Environmental conditions such as humidity, temperature, ventilation, and ultraviolet light can affect survival and transport. The virus also needs biological traits that allow efficient replication in tissues from which it can be expelled.

answer:
For a virus to spread efficiently through the air between humans, it generally needs to do several things. The first is to bind to receptors in the human upper respiratory tract. Avian influenza viruses mainly bind to alpha-2,3-linked sialic acids, which are found deep in the human lung and in birds' gut, while human-adapted influenza prefers alpha-2,6-linked sialic acids that line the upper airway. Without this shift, the virus has difficulty infecting the nose and throat, which is where it needs to replicate to be coughed or sneezed out.

The second requirement is that the virus replicates well at the cooler temperature of the human upper airway (around 33°C), rather than the warmer temperature in bird intestines. Changes in the polymerase protein, such as the PB2 E627K mutation, help with this.

Third, the virus has to be stable in aerosols and droplets. Factors like the stability of the hemagglutinin protein at the pH of respiratory fluids and the neuraminidase's balance with hemagglutinin's binding affect how well the virus survives in the air and how well it spreads.

Finally, it needs enough shedding in the upper airways to produce infectious particles, with a pattern of infection that causes people to cough or sneeze while they are still mobile.

Experiments on ferrets have shown that a small number of mutations can in principle confer airborne transmission, but whether this happens in nature is uncertain.

answer: To test for phages plate a 10-fold dilution series from 10 -1 to 10 -10 in soft agar overlays (0.75% agar in your broth of choice) with 100 ul of overnight bacterial culture and at some point(s) you should get clear countable plaques. This methodology has been around for a long time, since at least Gratia in 1936 1 and is very easy. Phages should also be filterable with a 0.1 um filter, but you'd need so much plasmid volume that it probably isn't worth it, though you could dilute the plasmid in buffer, filter, and then concentrate the DNA again. DNA extraction followed by gel separation is likely to be your best route. Any extraction protocol that contains either phenol (e.g. plain phenol-chloroform extraction) and/or guanidinium chloride (e.g. Trizol) should work well. This will extract both phage and plasmid DNA! As the above will also extract the phage DNA (assuming it is a DNA phage). When you transform the bacteria from this prep, the phage will be generated from its DNA. So, you need to separate the phage DNA from the plasmid. Generally, the easiest way to do this will be by size separation followed by gel-extraction. Simply run the DNA on a gel and perform a gel extraction on an appropriate sized band. You might want to consider digesting the plasmid with a single-site restriction endonuclease and re-circularizing after the extraction so as to allow you to get all your plasmid in a single band rather than spread across the various forms that plasmids can make, such as supercoiled, nicked and linear. You do need quite a bit of DNA to get a decent gel extraction; the returns are often less than 10% of input, but you only need a tiny amount to transform bacteria. Something in the nanogram range can work just fine for transformation. The caveat to the above is that your plasmid and the phage genome might be around the same size, so separation of the two on a gel could be difficult. In that case, you are likely to be best off simply amplifying your insert by PCR and ligating it into a new empty backbone. This is a simple process and generally very quick if your insert isn't enormous (>3000 bp) or you if you don't have some special needs with specific frame insertion requirements, or anything else which requires a bit of thought to perform. You can also amplify the backbone and use that too, but bigger PCRs can be difficult and cause errors in critical regions within the plasmid. A third option, if you knew which phage it was and had the genome, is that you could potentially choose a few restriction endonucleases that would digest the phage DNA but not the plasmid. Use 1-2 of those on your plasmid prep and re-transform. You'd want to be sure that your digest was successful, so doing a phage assay on the resulting culture would be essential. You could also potentially size separate and gel extract after the digest to remove any undigested phage DNA. If phages are present in your stock of competent bacteria, you are out of luck; you'll be best to get more bacteria from a clean source. You can either do this commercially through a company, or from a colleague, or from a cell bank. Apparently there are antibiotics that can inhibit phage infection, but I don't know how effective they will be, and most of the indicated substances will kill E. coli . See table 4 in this paper from Karczewska et al. 2023 2 . Phages easily contaminate equipment, so be sure to give your pipettes a thorough clean inside the barrel and on the tip ejector. 0.25% hypochlorite (made from bleach) will do nicely. Otherwise autoclave them if you can. Quaternary ammonium compounds can work too, but you need to meet the exposure times and they are not as effective. Reference: Gratia A. Numerical Relationships between Lysogenic Bacteria and Particles of Bacteriophage. Ann Inst Pasteur. 1936;57:652. Karczewska M, Strzelecki P, Szalewska-Pałasz A, Nowicki D. How to Tackle Bacteriophages: The Review of Approaches with Mechanistic Insight. Int J Mol Sci. 2023 Feb 23;24(5):4447. doi: 10.3390/ijms24054447. PMID: 36901878; PMCID: PMC10003480.

answer:
Phage contamination of plasmid stocks is a hard problem, and the most reliable fix is usually to start clean rather than try to purify the existing material. Some practical suggestions follow.

If the plasmid DNA is contaminated, standard purification may not help much because phage DNA and phage particles co-purify with it. Before discarding anything, however, test the stock by transforming it into a host and plating on a lawn, or spotting the plasmid prep on a lawn of indicator cells, to see if you get plaques. This confirms whether the plasmid stock is the source.

The most straightforward solution is to re-isolate the plasmid from a clean source. Retransform your plasmid into fresh, trusted cells, pick a single colony, and make new stocks. If you still have the original plasmid sequence, you can also re-synthesize or re-clone it. Avoid reusing any glycerol stocks or competent cells that might carry phage.

For decontaminating the working environment, bleach (about 10 percent, freshly made) or 70 percent ethanol followed by UV is more effective than Virkon for some phages. Autoclave media, replace stock solutions and pipette tips, and clean incubators, shakers, and water baths. Phages can persist on surfaces and in aerosols, so consider filtering media through 0.22 micron filters and using filter tips.

For the long term, consider using phage-resistant strains, such as ones with a deleted receptor, or adding calcium-free media, since many phages require calcium to adsorb to cells.

The short answer is that limb loss in snakes involved changes in the developmental genes and regulatory elements that control limb formation, and that those changes happened over a long period with a number of intermediate forms.

Fossil snakes show a gradual progression. Early snakes like Najash and Eupodophis still had hind limbs, and some, like Haasiophis, had small but well-formed hindlimbs. Modern boas and pythons retain tiny pelvic spurs, which are remnants of hind limbs. So the loss was not instantaneous, and in many lineages it is still incomplete, with limb remnants. Some snakes have lost these entirely.

On the genetic side, limb development depends on a signalling gene called Sonic hedgehog (Shh), which is turned on in the limb bud by a regulatory element called the ZRS. In snakes, the ZRS has accumulated mutations that disable it, which prevents Shh from being expressed and halts limb outgrowth. Mutating this enhancer in mice also produces limb reduction. Snake Hox gene expression has also been modified in ways that extend the trunk-like body and suppress forelimbs.

So complete loss is possible because limb formation depends on a few key switches. If these are disabled, no limb forms. In many other animals, those switches are still intact, so they get reduced limbs.
